def: A prompt together with a chosen (preferred) response and a rejected response, the basic unit of data for preference optimisation.
A three-stage method that fine-tunes a model on demonstrations, trains a reward model on human comparisons, then optimises the model against that reward with a KL penalty.
A network that reads a prompt and a response and outputs one number predicting how much people would prefer it, trained on comparisons.
A model in which the probability that one item beats another is the sigmoid of the difference of their hidden scores, used to turn comparisons into a reward loss.
The family of methods, including RLHF, DPO and their relatives, that tune a model towards responses people prefer using comparisons rather than demonstrations.
A method that trains the policy directly on preference pairs with a logistic loss on log-probability ratios against a reference, with no separate reward model or sampling loop.
In DPO, the quantity beta times the log of the policy's probability over the reference's probability for a response, which plays the role of the reward.
The coefficient that sets how far the policy may move from the reference: a small value allows large changes, a large value keeps the policy close.
The effect in DPO where the probability of the chosen response falls during training, because the loss only constrains the gap between chosen and rejected.
A DPO variant that uses a squared loss on the log-ratio margin, so the regulariser keeps working even when preference labels are deterministic.
A preference method that maximises a prospect-theory utility from single responses labelled desirable or undesirable, so it needs no pairs.
DPO in which the preference pairs are generated from the current policy's own samples and labelled by a reward model or judge, instead of coming from a fixed dataset.
